## Proof

**Setup and notation.** Let $f \geq 0$ be a locally integrable function on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $q > 1$. We compare two forms of the reverse Hölder inequality.

**Same-ball (strong) form.** There exists a constant $b > 0$ such that for every cube/ball $Q_R(x_0)$ with $R < R_0$:
$$\int_{Q_R(x_0)} f^q\,dx \;\leq\; b\left(\int_{Q_R(x_0)} f\,dx\right)^q. \tag{SH}$$

**Double-ball (weak) form.** There exists a constant $b' > 0$ such that for every $Q_R(x_0)$ with $2R < R_0$:
$$\int_{Q_R(x_0)} f^q\,dx \;\leq\; b'\left(\int_{Q_{2R}(x_0)} f\,dx\right)^q. \tag{DB}$$

---

### Why (SH) is stronger than (DB)

The same-ball inequality (SH) controls the $L^q$-mass of $f$ on a ball $Q_R$ using only the $L^1$-mass of $f$ on that **same, smaller** ball. The double-ball inequality (DB) only controls the $L^q$-mass on $Q_R$ using the $L^1$-mass on the **larger** ball $Q_{2R}$, which contains strictly more information (a larger domain of integration). Since $Q_R \subsetneq Q_{2R}$, the constraint imposed by (SH) is tighter: it demands that the $L^q$-behavior on a set be controlled by the $L^1$-behavior on that very set, not on a superset. Any function satisfying (SH) automatically satisfies (DB), but the converse fails in general—there are functions for which (DB) holds but (SH) does not.

---

### (SH) implies (DB)

Let $Q_R(x_0)$ be any ball with $2R < R_0$ (so that both $Q_R(x_0)$ and $Q_{2R}(x_0)$ are admissible). Since $R < R_0$, the same-ball inequality (SH) applies to $Q_R(x_0)$:

$$\int_{Q_R(x_0)} f^q\,dx \;\leq\; b\left(\int_{Q_R(x_0)} f\,dx\right)^q.$$

Now, since $Q_R(x_0) \subset Q_{2R}(x_0)$ and $f \geq 0$, monotonicity of the integral gives:

$$\int_{Q_R(x_0)} f\,dx \;\leq\; \int_{Q_{2R}(x_0)} f\,dx.$$

Since $q > 1$ and both integrals are non-negative, raising to the power $q$ preserves the inequality:

$$\left(\int_{Q_R(x_0)} f\,dx\right)^q \;\leq\; \left(\int_{Q_{2R}(x_0)} f\,dx\right)^q.$$

Chaining the two inequalities:

$$\int_{Q_R(x_0)} f^q\,dx \;\leq\; b\left(\int_{Q_R(x_0)} f\,dx\right)^q \;\leq\; b\left(\int_{Q_{2R}(x_0)} f\,dx\right)^q.$$

This is precisely (DB) with $b' = b$ (the same constant). $\quad\blacksquare$

---

### Remark on the averaged formulation

In many PDE references, the reverse Hölder inequality is stated with **averages** (Fazendeiro means) $\fint_{Q} g = \frac{1}{|Q|}\int_Q g$:

$$\fint_{Q_R} f^q \leq b\left(\fint_{Q_R} f\right)^q \quad\text{(SH-avg)}, \qquad \fint_{Q_R} f^q \leq b'\left(\fint_{Q_{2R}} f\right)^q \quad\text{(DB-avg)}.$$

Even in this formulation, (SH-avg) implies (DB-avg). Starting from (SH-avg):

$$\frac{1}{|Q_R|}\int_{Q_R} f^q \leq b\left(\frac{1}{|Q_R|}\int_{Q_R} f\right)^q = \frac{b}{|Q_R|^q}\left(\int_{Q_R} f\right)^q.$$

Using $\int_{Q_R} f \leq \int_{Q_{2R}} f$ and $|Q_{2R}| = 2^n|Q_R|$:

$$\fint_{Q_R} f^q \leq \frac{b}{|Q_R|^{q-1}}\left(\int_{Q_{2R}} f\right)^q = b\cdot 2^{nq}\cdot\frac{1}{|Q_{2R}|^q}\left(\int_{Q_{2R}} f\right)^q \cdot |Q_{2R}|^{q}\cdot|Q_R|^{1-q}.$$

Simplifying with $|Q_{2R}| = 2^n|Q_R|$:

$$\fint_{Q_R} f^q \leq b\cdot 2^{nq}\cdot\frac{1}{|Q_{2R}|^q}\left(\int_{Q_{2R}} f\right)^q \cdot \frac{|Q_{2R}|^q}{|Q_R|^q}\cdot|Q_R| = b\cdot 2^{nq}\cdot\frac{|Q_R|}{|Q_{2R}|^q}\left(\int_{Q_{2R}} f\right)^q = b\cdot 2^{nq}\left(\fint_{Q_{2R}} f\right)^q.$$

So (DB-avg) holds with $b' = b\cdot 2^{nq}$, a constant modified only by the dimensional factor $2^{nq}$. The key point remains: the same-ball form controls $f$ on a set using information from that set alone, making it the stronger, self-referential condition, from which the double-ball form follows by the elementary monotonicity $\int_{Q_R} f \leq \int_{Q_{2R}} f$.
